letter.title: Why a newsletter, and why now
paragraphs: Welcome to the first issue. The Center for Smart Cyber-Physical Systems was founded in October 2019 by five faculty who wanted to work on one problem together: making the systems people depend on, from the grid to the road to the hospital, secure and resilient as software and AI take over more of how they run. Seven years on, the center has 19 faculty across four colleges and 215 peer-reviewed papers, and every paper and award is listed on our website with a link to its source, so anyone can check the record.

This fall is a turning point. In October, the National Science Foundation's $2 million SUMMIT award begins, giving us a federated testbed that links UMass Lowell, NYU, and West Virginia University in one instrument for studying attacks on the grid and recovery from them. This fall we are applying to the university for full research center status, and we are broadening what we do to put people in the loop: operators, drivers, patients, and the trust between them and the automation they work with.

Each month this newsletter will carry one student story, one faculty story, and one project, along with what was published and funded. If you are a student looking for a group, a company looking for a testbed, or a colleague looking for a collaborator, the last page tells you how to reach us. Thank you for reading.

project_spotlight.title: SUMMIT: attack, defend, and recover the grid
project_spotlight.deck: A $2.0 million NSF Major Research Instrumentation award builds a three-university instrument where real control, network, and security hardware closes the loop with a real-time simulation of the Northeast grid.
project_spotlight.figure_caption: SUMMIT's architecture: the UMass Lowell main site, a wide-area software-defined network, and the NYU and WVU federation sites.

p: Grid cybersecurity research has a practical problem: you cannot attack a real grid to see what happens, and a software simulation leaves out the relays, controllers, and network devices where attacks land. SUMMIT closes that gap. NSF's Major Research Instrumentation program funds it at $2.0 million (award #2511635; UMass Lowell share $1.56 million, with subawards to NYU and West Virginia University) from October 2026 through September 2029.

At the core, RTDS NovaCor real-time digital simulators run grid models fast enough to drive real relays, controllers, and network devices in closed loop, and every power component lives inside the simulation. Around them at UMass Lowell sit disturbance-injection equipment, a network emulator for latency, loss, and attack scenarios, optical, RF, and FPGA equipment, and GPS-synchronized control and protection gear. Software-defined network links connect the three sites over the public Internet.

SUMMIT supports four ways of working: distributed hardware-in-the-loop simulation; Internet-in-the-loop simulation, where the network between the sites is part of every experiment; distributed digital twins across the RTDS and OPAL-RT simulators; and the central objective, a federated platform that delivers hardware-in-the-loop Simulation-as-a-Service to collaborators who never touch the hardware.

sections.h: Phase 1, and who it is for
p: Phase 1 models the Northeast's backbone transmission grid at proof-of-concept scale, ready to grow to regional and national models in Phase 2. PI Vinod Vokkarane leads with Co-PIs Orlando Arias and Lewis Tseng (UMass Lowell), Yuzhang Lin (NYU), and Anurag Srivastava (WVU), and senior personnel Yan Luo, Seung Woo Son, and Christopher Niezrecki. A postdoctoral position is open, and collaborators can propose experiments as the instrument opens in 2026 to 2027.

project_spotlight.pull: Every power component lives inside the simulation. That is what lets the testbed stay safe, repeatable, and free of power hardware on site, and it is what lets three universities share one instrument.

faculty_spotlight.title: Sukesh Aghara: the Commonwealth's nuclear roadmap and the center's energy thrust
faculty_spotlight.deck: A center co-founder who now advises the Chancellor on nuclear energy strategy, leads the Massachusetts Advanced Nuclear and Fusion Energy Roadmap, and directs the laboratory where nuclear security meets cyber-physical systems.
faculty_spotlight.figure_caption: Sukesh Aghara, Professor of Chemical and Nuclear Engineering and Senior Advisor to the Chancellor on Nuclear Energy Strategies.

p: When the center was founded in 2019, Sukesh Aghara was one of its five co-founders and its founding co-director for energy. He still leads the nuclear energy and security thrust. What has changed is the scale of the questions he is asked to answer. In October 2025 he was asked to lead the Massachusetts Advanced Nuclear and Fusion Energy Roadmap, the Commonwealth's plan for how advanced reactors and fusion fit its energy future. In 2026 UMass Lowell named him Senior Advisor to the Chancellor on Nuclear Energy Strategies, after five years as the Francis College of Engineering's Associate Dean for Research and eight as director of the Nuclear Engineering Program.

Aghara directs the Integrated Nuclear Security and Safeguards Laboratory, INSSL, which sits alongside the UMass Lowell research reactor. The lab has radiation detectors and cyber-physical testbeds, and its work on the cybersecurity of nuclear facilities, safeguards verification, and advanced reactor modeling is supported by federal agencies including the National Nuclear Security Administration. He also co-directs the Intercontinental Nuclear Institute, a partnership with the International Atomic Energy Agency that trains the next generation of nuclear security professionals. Both are where the center's cyber-physical work meets the nuclear world: a reactor's control and protection systems are cyber-physical systems whose failure has physical consequences.

He is the editor of The Oxford Handbook of Nuclear Security, published by Oxford University Press, with chapters of his own on cybersecurity for nuclear facilities and on security for next-generation reactors. His recent work ranges from stochastic methods for safeguards inspection to a June 2026 paper in Energy Reports, with Korinek, Annadevula, and Skoda, on phasing clean alternatives into a university campus's central heating. He chaired the Nuclear Engineering Department Heads Organization in 2024 to 2025.

On September 30, UMass Lowell hosts the New England Governors' Nuclear Energy Summit at the Rist Institute. For the center, it is where the SUMMIT testbed meets the nuclear community: a plant's connection to the grid can be tested in the instrument before the plant is built.
